title: Wood v. Lucy, Lady Duff-Gordon
lead: An exclusive endorsement agency produces a lawsuit over whether the marketer undertook to do any marketing.

actors.name: Lucy, Lady Duff-Gordon
actors.role: Fashion creator who granted exclusive commercial rights and retained approval of proposed endorsements.

actors.name: Otis F. Wood
actors.role: Marketer who accepted the exclusive agency and sued over independent endorsements.

proceedings: Special Term denied Lady Duff-Gordon’s challenge to the complaint.
The Appellate Division granted judgment on the pleadings for her.
The Court of Appeals restored the denial of that motion; breach and damages remained undecided.
limits: The court tested a complaint on the pleadings. Wood’s performance and Lady Duff-Gordon’s breach were allegations accepted for that purpose, not findings after a trial. No later merits result is supplied.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with the complete effective canonical brief; no new independent opinion verification claimed.

sections.title: A fashion creator gives Wood an exclusive commercial role
sections.cue: What did each party bring to the arrangement, and what rights did the agreement grant?
paragraphs: Lucy, Lady Duff-Gordon was a prominent fashion creator. Manufacturers paid for the value of her approval, and her own fabrics, garments, parasols, and other designs gained commercial value when marketed under her name. Otis F. Wood had a business organization suited to placing endorsements. Their signed agreement put that organization to work in an exclusive agency.

Subject to Lady Duff-Gordon’s approval, Wood received the exclusive right to place her endorsement on designs created by others. He also received the exclusive right to sell her own designs or license others to manufacture and market them. The arrangement began April 1, 1915, lasted at least one year, and continued from year to year unless terminated on ninety days’ notice. She therefore committed a defined channel of commercial activity to Wood for a defined period while retaining approval of proposed transactions.

sections.title: The agreement ties her income to Wood’s transactions
sections.cue: Which express obligations made the disputed efforts promise plausible?
paragraphs: Lady Duff-Gordon was to receive one-half of the profits and revenues from the contracts Wood made under the agency. Wood expressly undertook to collect the money, remit her share, and account monthly for all money received. He also promised to obtain patents, copyrights, and trademarks when his judgment found them useful to protect affected names, ideas, and articles. The writing recited that he possessed an organization adapted to placing endorsements she approved.

The agreement did not include an express sentence saying that Wood must use reasonable efforts to obtain deals. That omission later became the focus of the litigation. Read literally in isolation, duties to collect and divide receipts might arise only if Wood happened to arrange a transaction. Read as an operating business arrangement, however, exclusivity and a revenue-dependent return could imply an obligation to try to generate the transactions from which both sides expected compensation.

sections.title: Wood alleges that Lady Duff-Gordon bypassed the agency
sections.cue: What did Wood allege, and why was the court not yet deciding whether it happened?
paragraphs: Wood alleged that he fully performed his own duties. He alleged that Lady Duff-Gordon nevertheless independently endorsed fabrics, dresses, and millinery, received valuable consideration, and kept the proceeds while excluding him. He sued for breach of the exclusive arrangement and set out the signed agreement in full in his complaint.

Lady Duff-Gordon challenged the legal sufficiency of that complaint through the New York pleading procedure described as a demurrer and a motion for judgment on the pleadings. For that purpose, her challenge accepted the well-pleaded allegations and argued that the writing created no enforceable obligation supporting her promises. It did not establish at a trial that Wood had failed to work or that she had made the alleged independent endorsements.

sections.title: Two lower courts disagree about the missing express promise
sections.cue: Why did the Appellate Division give judgment to Lady Duff-Gordon?
paragraphs: Special Term denied Lady Duff-Gordon’s motion, allowing Wood’s claim to proceed. The Appellate Division, First Department, unanimously reversed on April 20, 1917. Justice Davis read the writing as requiring Wood to collect and divide revenue only when he elected to arrange an endorsement, sale, or license. Because the agreement did not expressly require him to procure any transaction, that court found no mutuality or consideration and granted judgment on the pleadings to Lady Duff-Gordon.

Wood appealed to New York’s Court of Appeals. The appeal was argued on November 14, 1917. The question before that court was whether the complete writing implied an enforceable reasonable-efforts undertaking, so that the exclusivity promise had consideration and Wood’s complaint stated a contract claim.

sections.title: Cardozo reads the promises as one commercial exchange
sections.cue: How do exclusivity, compensation, and Wood’s other duties support the implied obligation?
paragraphs: Judge Cardozo read the recitals, exclusivity grants, duration, compensation formula, and administrative duties together. Lady Duff-Gordon had placed the relevant marketing opportunities within Wood’s sole channel for at least a year. Her contractual return depended on revenue from his efforts. Wood’s acceptance of that exclusive position therefore carried an undertaking to make reasonable efforts to operate the channel. Without such an undertaking, her commercial grant and the agreed source of her compensation would be left dependent on his unrestricted choice to do nothing.

The recital about Wood’s adapted business organization identified the capacity the parties intended him to deploy. His express duties to collect and divide money, give monthly accounts, and secure intellectual-property protection presupposed transactions, receipts, and protectable interests. Those provisions reinforced the obligation to make reasonable efforts to bring the underlying business into existence. The court drew an obligation from the particular writing and its intended operation.

Reasonable efforts required diligent pursuit of the undertaking in light of the enterprise, market opportunities, the parties’ purpose, and Wood’s represented capacity. It left room for business judgment about particular deals, which remained subject to Lady Duff-Gordon’s approval. It did not promise commercial success. An unreasonable failure to develop the business could expose Wood to liability, giving his undertaking the legal force necessary to support her reciprocal grant.

Cardozo’s interpretation drew on the business-efficacy reasoning associated with The Moorcock and New York exclusive-agency cases. It answered the intermediate court’s focus on the absence of an express procurement sentence by explaining the commitment conveyed by the agreement as a whole.

sources.pinpoint: Reasoning: whole agreement, exclusivity, capacity, compensation, downstream duties, implied term, and historical setting

sections.title: The complaint survives, leaving the merits to later proceedings
sections.cue: State the exact result and the questions the appellate decision did not decide.
paragraphs: On December 4, 1917, a four-judge Court of Appeals majority reversed the Appellate Division and affirmed Special Term, with costs in both appellate courts. Judges Cuddeback, McLaughlin, and Andrews joined Cardozo. Chief Judge Hiscock and Judges Chase and Crane dissented without separate opinions. The supplied source reports no written dissenting rationale to add to the story.

Wood’s claim could proceed because the implied reasonable-efforts promise supplied consideration. He still had to prove his own performance, Lady Duff-Gordon’s breach, causation, and damages. She could contest whether the challenged transactions fell within the agency and whether Wood had met his implied duty. The Court of Appeals did not award him a demonstrated amount of lost profits.

For later study, UCC § 2-306(2) states a parallel exclusive-dealing rule for goods, ordinarily requiring best efforts by the seller to supply and the buyer to promote. That later provision was not the law Cardozo applied in 1917. The historical decision illustrates how a court can derive the minimum performance commitment that gives an exclusive commercial exchange its intended operation by examining every term and recital together.
